analysis.one_liner: Bars colleges from forcing athletes to sign COVID-19 liability waivers or lose scholarships for sitting out.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by two Democratic senators in June 2020 and died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any additional cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2020 push to restart college sports amid the pandemic, this bill would have required colleges to protect athletes: no liability waivers for COVID-19, no canceling scholarships of athletes who sat out over virus concerns, notification of positive cases, compliance with CDC health guidelines, and a right to sue in state court for violations. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, who generally cannot reject a liability waiver or quit their sport without losing their scholarship, would gain protection from being forced to accept COVID-19 risk, guaranteed notification of positive cases, and the ability to sue colleges that violate the rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: College athletes playing during the pandemic

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits colleges from requiring athletes to sign waivers releasing the school from liability for COVID-19 in any sporting activity.
Bars colleges from canceling a scholarship or other financial aid of an athlete who skips team activities due to COVID-19 concerns.
Requires colleges to notify all athletes when an athlete or athletic-department staffer tests positive, without identifying the person.
Directs the CDC to develop COVID-19 health and safety guidelines for college athletic departments within 90 days and requires schools to follow them.
Creates a private right of action in state court, including for punitive damages, letting athletes enforce the law against their own schools.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities would bear compliance costs and lose the ability to shield themselves from COVID-19 lawsuits through waivers, and could face damages suits; athletic departments would bear the cost of testing, notification, and CDC-guideline compliance.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action includes punitive damages, which schools would argue drives costly litigation against already strained university budgets.

The bill does not address the underlying financial driver of pandemic college sports: billions in broadcast and conference revenue that gave schools strong incentive to play on regardless of health rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are modest, targeted, and directly aimed at a group of students with little bargaining power; the main cost falls on universities that generate substantial revenue from athlete performance. The main design criticism is enforcement through state courts rather than federal agencies, but the core provisions are straightforward safety rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP committee on June 30, 2020, and received no further action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on June 30, 2020, with Sen. Cory Booker as an original cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever taken on the bill before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Universities and athletic conferences that wanted to resume play without federal COVID-19 safety mandates or a new right for athletes to sue them were better off because the bill never advanced; athletes were left with no federal protections for the 2020-21 season.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Universities playing sports without federal COVID-19 rules

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar COVID-19 liability waivers and scholarship penalties for college athletes.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both senators who supported it were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no formal partisan breakdown exists.

industries.industry: College athletics and universities with revenue sports
industries.note: The bill would force athletic departments to comply with CDC COVID-19 guidelines, disclose positive cases, drop liability waivers, and keep scholarships intact for athletes who sit out — costs and legal exposure they avoided by continuing to play without federal rules. College sports is a multi-billion-dollar enterprise in which the athletes themselves are unpaid.
